q: What is a Lead in Salesforce and how does the lead process work?
alt: Explain the lead lifecycle in Sales Cloud
What is a lead and what is a lead process?
how do leads work in salesforce
What are lead statuses used for?
a: A Lead is a person or company that has shown interest but isn't qualified yet as a real sales opportunity. The lead process is just the set of Lead Status picklist values it moves through, like Open, Contacted, Working, Qualified and Unqualified. Say a laptop seller gets a web form from an office manager asking about fifty laptops. That comes in as a lead, an assignment rule routes it to a rep or a queue, and the rep calls and moves it to Contacted, then Working. Once budget and timing check out, it's Qualified, and the rep converts it into an Account, a Contact and, if there's a real deal, an Opportunity. Leads can also come in from imports, campaigns or integrations. One thing to remember: if business units qualify leads differently, you can have separate lead processes and attach each one through a record type. Before building any of it, I get sales and marketing to agree in writing what Qualified actually means, because that definition drives every conversion and pipeline report after it.
points: Lead = unqualified prospect, separate object from Contact
Lead process = set of Lead Status values, tied to record types
At least one status must be marked Converted
End of the lifecycle is conversion or disqualification

q: What happens when you convert a lead?
alt: Explain lead conversion in Salesforce
Which records get created on lead conversion?
what happens to the lead after you convert it
Lead convert kya karta hai, which objects are created?
a: Conversion is a one-way step, so I treat it carefully. When I convert a lead, Salesforce creates an Account, a Contact and, optionally, an Opportunity from the lead data. Say a rep converts a lead for Priya from a small accounting firm. If that firm already exists as an account, I'd link the lead to it instead of creating a new one, and the same for an existing contact. That's how you avoid duplicates. The lead itself isn't deleted. It's marked IsConverted true, becomes read-only for normal users, and keeps the new record Ids in ConvertedAccountId, ConvertedContactId and ConvertedOpportunityId. Priya's campaign memberships and open activities move over to her contact. The gotcha is fields: standard fields map automatically, but custom fields only carry over if you map them in the lead field mapping setup. On my teams, any new custom Lead field has to come with a mapping decision in the same story, otherwise data quietly gets lost at conversion.
points: Creates Account, Contact and optional Opportunity
Can merge into existing Account or Contact
Lead stays in the system, flagged IsConverted, read-only
Custom fields need Map Lead Fields setup

q: A custom field on Lead is not carrying over to the Contact after conversion. Why, and how do you fix it?
alt: How does lead field mapping work for custom fields?
Custom lead field data lost after converting lead
Where do you map lead fields to account contact opportunity?
lead custom field not copying on convert
a: Almost always this is a missing field mapping. Standard lead fields map on their own, but a custom field only carries over if you map it. I'd go to the Lead object's Fields and Relationships, open Map Lead Fields, and map it to a matching custom field on Account, Contact or Opportunity. Say the lead has a custom Preferred Laptop Model text field, 100 characters long. The contact field has to be a compatible type, like text to text, or picklist to picklist or text, and at least as long, so 100 or more. Each lead field can map to only one target field, so you can't send that one field to both the contact and the opportunity. If the mapping is already there, I check field-level security on the target field, and then whether a trigger or flow on the contact is overwriting the value right after conversion. To stop it recurring, I add Map Lead Fields to the definition of done for any new Lead field, and I check it in review.
points: Map Lead Fields is under Lead object setup
Target must be a compatible data type and length
One lead field maps to one target field
Also check FLS and automation overwriting the value

q: What are lead assignment rules?
alt: How do you auto assign leads to reps or queues?
Explain assignment rules for leads
how many lead assignment rules can be active
How does Salesforce decide who owns a new lead?
a: Lead assignment rules set the owner of a lead automatically, either a user or a queue, based on criteria like country, industry or lead source. Only one lead assignment rule can be active at a time, but it can have many entries, and Salesforce checks them in order and stops at the first match. For example, entry one says country is India, send to the India queue. Entry two says industry is Education, send to Ravi. A lead from a school in India hits entry one first, so it goes to the India queue, not to Ravi. That's why the order matters, and it's the first thing I review when someone asks for a new entry: where it sits can silently change who gets every other lead. The rules fire for web-to-lead, imports with the option ticked, API inserts that pass the assignment rule header, and manual creates when the user checks the assign-using-active-rule box. If nothing matches, the lead goes to the default lead owner set in Lead Settings.
points: One active rule, many ordered entries, first match wins
Owner can be a user or a queue
Default lead owner catches leads with no match
In Apex use Database.DMLOptions assignmentRuleHeader

q: What is Web-to-Lead and what are its limitations?
alt: How do you capture leads from a website form?
Explain web to lead
web to lead daily limit
How does a website form create leads in Salesforce?
a: Web-to-Lead generates an HTML form from Setup that posts straight into Salesforce and creates a lead. You pick the fields, Salesforce gives you the HTML, and the web team puts it on the site. You can turn on reCAPTCHA to cut spam, and assignment and auto-response rules can fire on those leads. The big limit is a daily cap of 500 leads. Say a laptop seller runs a sale banner and gets 800 enquiries in one day. The extra 300 aren't created as leads that day; they're held, and the default creator gets an email with them. There's also no built-in duplicate prevention on the form, so the same person submitting twice gives you two leads, and validation and file upload support are limited. For that kind of volume or a richer form, I'd push the team away from Web-to-Lead and use an integration through the API, or a Flow-based form on an Experience Cloud site. I'd also check the expected peak volume with marketing up front, because the 500 cap usually surfaces on the busiest campaign day.
points: Generates HTML form that posts to Salesforce
Daily limit of 500 web-to-lead submissions
Enable reCAPTCHA to fight spam
Assignment and auto-response rules can fire

q: How do you convert leads in Apex using Database.convertLead?
alt: Write Apex code to convert a lead
convert lead programmatically
What is the LeadConvert class used for?
How do you bulk convert leads with Apex without creating an opportunity?
a: My standard here is always bulk conversion. I build a list of Database.LeadConvert objects, one per lead, and pass the whole list to Database.convertLead in a single call so it stays bulkified. For each one I set the lead Id and a converted status. That status has to be a Lead Status value marked as converted, so I query LeadStatus where IsConverted is true instead of hard-coding it. To merge into existing records I call setAccountId or setContactId, I use setDoNotCreateOpportunity when there's no deal yet, and setOwnerId to change the owner. Say a nightly job converts 200 qualified leads and three of them fail a validation rule on Contact. I use the allOrNone false version and loop through the LeadConvertResult list to log those three errors. That matters because validation rules on Account, Contact or Opportunity can fail individual conversions. In code review I specifically look for a hard-coded converted status or convertLead inside a loop; both get sent back.
points: One LeadConvert per lead, one convertLead call for the list
Converted status comes from LeadStatus where IsConverted = true
setAccountId / setContactId to avoid duplicates
Check LeadConvertResult for per-record errors

q: Users are getting an error when they try to convert a lead. How would you troubleshoot it?
alt: Lead conversion failing, what do you check?
Why does lead convert throw a validation error?
lead convert button giving error
Common reasons lead conversion fails
a: I start from the target objects, because most lead conversion errors actually come from there. First I read the error and see whether it's about the Account, Contact or Opportunity. The usual causes are a validation rule or required field on one of those that the lead data doesn't satisfy, a trigger or flow on the new records throwing an exception, or a duplicate rule blocking the new account or contact. For example, if the message says Region is required on Opportunity, the lead probably has no region, so the new opportunity can't save. I also check that the user has create permission on all three objects, that the Convert Leads permission is enabled, and that the lead process has a converted status. Sometimes the fix is a bypass for validation rules during conversion, using the IsConverted context or a lead conversion-specific check. I'd be careful with that bypass though: it has to be narrow and documented, so we're not weakening data quality just to make the error go away.
points: Errors usually come from Account, Contact or Opportunity rules
Check required fields, validation rules, triggers, duplicate rules
User needs Convert Leads permission and create access
Lead process must have a converted status

q: What is the difference between a Business Account and a Person Account?
alt: When would you use Person Accounts?
Explain person accounts in Salesforce
B2B vs B2C account model
person account versus account and contact
a: A Business Account is a company, and the people who work there are separate Contacts linked to it. That's the classic B2B model. A Person Account is an individual customer, like in retail banking or insurance, and it combines account and contact into one record, so personal fields like birthdate show right on the account page. For example, a laptop seller that sells to companies uses business accounts, but if it also sells direct to students, each student could be a person account. Under the hood a Person Account still has a hidden contact record, and IsPersonAccount and PersonContactId tell you which is which. Person Accounts have to be enabled and need a person account record type. The big gotcha is that once enabled, they can't be turned off, so I always treat it as a design decision, not a quick setting. I'd want the business model confirmed, test it in a sandbox, and check how it affects integrations and reports before anyone enables it in production.
points: Business Account = company with related Contacts (B2B)
Person Account = individual, account and contact combined (B2C)
Has a hidden contact; check IsPersonAccount
Enabling Person Accounts cannot be reversed

q: What are opportunity stages, and how do they relate to probability and forecast category?
alt: Explain opportunity stage, probability and forecast category
How does stage drive forecast category?
what is opportunity stage name
What happens to probability when I change the stage?
a: Opportunity Stage shows where a deal is in the sales cycle, like Prospecting, Qualification, Proposal, Negotiation, Closed Won and Closed Lost. Each stage value is set up with a default probability, a forecast category such as Pipeline, Best Case, Commit, Closed or Omitted, and a type of open, closed won or closed lost. When a rep changes the stage, probability and forecast category default from that setup, though users with edit access can override them. Say a rep moves a laptop deal to Negotiation, and Negotiation is set up as Commit. The deal now shows in the manager's Commit number. If the rep overrides it back to Best Case, the forecast follows the override. That's the key point: forecasts and pipeline reports read the forecast category, so getting the stage setup right is what keeps forecasting accurate. That's why I'd agree the stage-to-category mapping with sales leadership rather than letting admins pick defaults.
points: Stage values set default probability and forecast category
Forecast categories: Pipeline, Best Case, Commit, Closed, Omitted
Each stage is Open, Closed/Won or Closed/Lost
Forecasts read forecast category, not stage

q: What is a Sales Process and how is it connected to record types?
alt: How do you show different stages to different teams?
Explain sales process in Salesforce
sales process vs record type
Can two sales teams have different opportunity stages?
a: A Sales Process is a subset of the Opportunity Stage picklist values that one team uses. You create the sales process, pick which stages it includes, and assign it to an opportunity record type. Users get that record type through their profile or permission set, so they only see their own stages. For example, a laptop seller's renewals team might only need Prospecting, Negotiation, Closed Won and Closed Lost, while the new-business team uses the full list. That's two sales processes on two record types, and each rep sees just their stages. It's the same idea as lead processes for leads and support processes for cases. On top of that I usually add a Path with key fields and guidance per stage, so reps know what to fill in before moving forward. I try to keep the number of sales processes small, since each extra one adds record types, reports and automation the team has to maintain.
points: Sales process = subset of StageName values
Assigned through opportunity record types
Record types assigned via profile or permission set
Path adds guidance and key fields per stage

q: Explain Products, Price Books and Price Book Entries.
alt: What is a price book entry?
How do products and price books work together?
standard price book vs custom price book
What is the relationship between Product2 and Pricebook2?
a: Product2 is the item you sell. A Price Book, Pricebook2, is a list of prices, and PricebookEntry is the junction that says this product costs this much in this price book, and in multi-currency orgs, in this currency. Say a laptop seller has a 14-inch business laptop. It has a standard price in the Standard Price Book, and there's a custom Partner price book with a lower price for distributors. Every org has one Standard Price Book, and a product needs a standard price before you can add it to any custom price book. An opportunity is tied to one price book, so a partner deal using the Partner book only lets the rep pick from active entries in that book. Adding the laptop creates an OpportunityLineItem record. Custom price books are used for things like regional, partner or volume pricing. I keep the price book count deliberate, because every new book is another set of entries someone has to keep current.
points: Product2 = item, Pricebook2 = price list, PricebookEntry = price of a product in a book
Standard price required before custom price book entry
One price book per opportunity
Adding products creates OpportunityLineItem records

q: A rep says they cannot find a product when adding products to an opportunity. What would you check?
alt: Product not showing in Add Products on opportunity
Why can't users see a product in the price book?
add products button not listing my product
product missing when adding opportunity line items
a: This is nearly always data setup, not a bug, so I'd go step by step. First, is the product itself active, and does it have an active price book entry in the price book the opportunity is using? The opportunity can only show products from its own price book. Second, in a multi-currency org, the entry has to exist in the opportunity's currency. Third, the price book must be active, and the user needs sharing access to it, since price books have their own sharing. And if the product was just created, it needs a standard price before it can be added to a custom price book. For example, a rep on a EUR deal using the Partner price book can't find a new docking station. Often it turns out the dock was only priced in USD, or only in the Standard Price Book, so it simply doesn't show up for that deal. Once I find it, I'd give product ops a short checklist for new products so the team isn't fixing the same thing every launch.
points: Product active and price book entry active
Entry must be in the opportunity's price book
Entry must match the opportunity currency
User needs access to the price book

q: What are product schedules on opportunity products?
alt: Explain quantity and revenue schedules
How do you spread revenue over months on an opportunity?
what is a revenue schedule in salesforce
How do you handle a deal that bills monthly over a year?
a: Product schedules let you spread an opportunity product's quantity or revenue across dates instead of booking it all on the close date. A quantity schedule spreads the units, and a revenue schedule spreads the amount. For example, a company orders 100 laptops but wants 25 delivered each quarter, so that's a quantity schedule over four quarters. If the same customer pays for a support contract monthly over twelve months, that's a revenue schedule. You enable schedules in Setup, then turn them on per product, and you can set a default schedule on the product or let reps establish it on the line item. They're stored as OpportunityLineItemSchedule records. I'd only turn schedules on after finance confirms they'll actually use them, because it's extra data for reps to maintain. It's useful when finance wants to see when revenue actually lands, and collaborative forecasts can use a schedule date based forecast type.
points: Quantity schedule spreads units, revenue schedule spreads amount
Enable in Setup, then per product
Stored as OpportunityLineItemSchedule
Can drive schedule-date based forecasts

q: What are Quotes in Sales Cloud and what does quote syncing do?
alt: Explain quotes and quote templates
How do you generate a quote PDF from an opportunity?
what is quote sync
Can an opportunity have multiple quotes?
a: Quotes let reps present prices, discounts and products to a customer from an opportunity. One opportunity can have many quotes, but only one can be synced with it at a time. When a quote is synced, its line items and the opportunity products stay in sync both ways. Say a rep sends a school two options: Quote A with 40 laptops, and Quote B with 40 laptops plus bags. The school picks B, so the rep syncs Quote B, and now the opportunity products match it. Change a quantity on either side and the other one follows. Quote templates control the PDF layout, with sections for line items, terms and branding, and the rep can save the PDF to the quote or email it directly. If the company needs complex pricing rules, bundles and approvals, that's usually where Revenue Cloud comes in instead of standard quotes. That's the call I'd make with stakeholders early: standard quotes are cheap to run, so I only recommend moving up when the pricing really needs it.
points: Many quotes per opportunity, only one synced
Sync keeps quote lines and opportunity products aligned
Quote templates define the PDF layout
Complex pricing goes to Revenue Cloud

q: How does Collaborative Forecasting work?
alt: Explain forecast types, categories and forecast hierarchy
How do forecasts roll up in Salesforce?
collaborative forecasts setup steps
What is a forecast type?
a: In short, Collaborative Forecasts rolls up opportunity data by forecast category and time period through a forecast hierarchy. A forecast type defines what you forecast: the source object, like opportunities, opportunity splits, product families or territories, the measure, like revenue or quantity, and the date used, like close date. The hierarchy is usually the role hierarchy, or the territory hierarchy if you forecast by territory, and you enable users as forecast managers so their numbers roll up. You choose monthly or quarterly periods and whether rollups are cumulative, so Commit includes Closed, and so on. For example, if a rep has 50,000 closed and 30,000 in Commit this quarter, a cumulative Commit shows 80,000. Her manager sees that roll up with the rest of the team, can adjust it, and can compare it against quotas. The decision I'd settle with sales leadership first is cumulative or not, because changing it later confuses everyone reading the numbers.
points: Forecast type = object + measure + date
Rolls up through role or territory hierarchy
Forecast managers must be enabled per user
Monthly or quarterly periods, cumulative rollups optional

q: What are forecast adjustments and quotas?
alt: Can a manager change a rep's forecast number?
Explain manager adjustments and owner adjustments
how are quotas loaded in salesforce forecasts
difference between adjusted and unadjusted forecast
a: Adjustments let people change the forecast number without touching the opportunities underneath. A manager adjustment lets a forecast manager override a subordinate's rollup or their own, and an owner adjustment lets a rep adjust their own forecast. Both have to be enabled. For example, a rep's Commit rolls up to 80,000, but her manager thinks that's too optimistic because one big laptop order looks likely to slip, so he adjusts it to 60,000. The original 80,000 is still kept, so you can compare both, and no opportunity was edited. Quotas are the target amounts per user and period, stored as ForecastingQuota records, and you usually load them with Data Loader or the API. Once quotas are in, the forecast page shows attainment, so managers can see who's on track. I'd own the quota load as a scheduled, checked process each period, since a wrong quota file undermines trust in the whole forecast.
points: Manager and owner adjustments must be enabled
Adjustments do not change opportunity data
Unadjusted and adjusted values both visible
Quotas stored in ForecastingQuota, loaded via Data Loader or API

q: Explain Enterprise Territory Management and its main components.
alt: What is ETM in Salesforce?
How does territory management work?
territory model, territory type and territory hierarchy explained
Why use territories instead of role hierarchy for sharing?
a: Enterprise Territory Management lets you organize accounts and users by sales territory, separate from the role hierarchy, and grant access based on that. The top level is a Territory Model, which can be in planning, active or archived state. Only one model can be active at a time, so you can build and preview next year's model before switching. Inside the model you have Territory Types with a priority, the Territories themselves in a hierarchy, and account assignment rules that place accounts by criteria like billing state or industry. For example, a laptop seller might have North and South territories, with a rule that puts every account with billing state Karnataka into South. Users are assigned to territories with a role, and each territory defines the access users get to accounts, opportunities, cases and contacts. Opportunities can be assigned to territories through a filter-based Apex class. The planning state is what I lean on as a lead: we build and preview the new model with sales ops before activation, so nobody loses access to their accounts on day one.
points: Model states: planning, active, archived; one active at a time
Territory types, territories, assignment rules
Objects: Territory2Model, Territory2, UserTerritory2Association, ObjectTerritory2Association
Sharing is driven by territory access levels

q: An account belongs to two territories. How do you decide which territory an opportunity should belong to?
alt: How does opportunity territory assignment work in ETM?
Opportunity territory assignment filter Apex
account in multiple territories which one does the opportunity get
How do you auto assign territory to opportunities?
a: This is a business decision first and code second. An account can sit in several territories, but an opportunity has only one Territory2Id, so you need a rule to pick one. Salesforce supports filter-based opportunity territory assignment, where you write an Apex class implementing the TerritoryMgmt.OpportunityTerritory2AssignmentFilter interface. Salesforce's default sample picks the account's territory with the highest territory type priority, and if there's a tie it leaves it blank. Say a hospital group sits in both an Enterprise territory and a Healthcare territory. I'd agree the business rule first, for example product line decides, so server deals go to Enterprise and laptop deals go to Healthcare. Then I implement that in the filter class, register it in Territory Settings, and run it on new opportunities and as a bulk job when the model changes. Reps can still change it manually if their access allows. I'd also get the rule signed off by sales ops, because it decides who gets credit for the deal.
points: Opportunity has one territory; account can have many
Implement TerritoryMgmt.OpportunityTerritory2AssignmentFilter
Default sample uses territory type priority
Agree the business rule before coding

q: What are Campaigns and Campaign Members?
alt: How do campaigns work in Sales Cloud?
What is a campaign member status?
explain campaign hierarchy
How do you track which leads came from an event?
a: A Campaign is a marketing effort, like a webinar, trade show or email blast, and it tracks budget, expected and actual cost, and results. Campaign Members link leads or contacts to it, and each member has a status like Sent or Responded. You can customize those statuses per campaign and mark which ones count as responded. For example, a laptop seller runs a webinar with statuses Invited, Registered and Attended, and only Attended is flagged as responded. Campaigns can sit in a hierarchy, so a parent Back to School program rolls up results from the webinar, the email blast and the trade show under it. Opportunities can have a Primary Campaign Source, and campaign reports show how many leads, responses, opportunities and won amount each campaign generated. I'd set a team standard for member statuses and the hierarchy early, otherwise every marketer invents their own and the reports stop comparing.
points: Campaign = marketing initiative with budget and results
CampaignMember links a Lead or Contact
Member statuses are custom per campaign, with a Responded flag
Campaign hierarchy rolls up stats

q: What is Campaign Influence?
alt: How do you attribute revenue to multiple campaigns?
Explain customizable campaign influence
primary campaign source vs campaign influence
Which campaigns influenced this opportunity?
a: Campaign Influence shows every campaign that contributed to an opportunity, not just the single primary campaign source. With Customizable Campaign Influence, Salesforce can automatically associate campaigns to an opportunity when contacts with opportunity contact roles were members of those campaigns, within a time frame you set. Each association gets a revenue share based on an attribution model. For example, on a laptop deal, the IT head and the finance contact are both contact roles. The IT head attended a webinar and the finance contact was in an email campaign, both inside the window, so both campaigns get linked to the opportunity. The default model gives the credit to the primary campaign source, and you can add custom models, while Account Engagement, formerly Pardot, adds multi-touch models like first touch, last touch and even distribution, where those two campaigns would split the credit equally. Marketing uses this to answer how much pipeline each campaign really influenced. The trade-off I'd explain to marketing is that the time frame and model choice change the numbers a lot, so we agree them once and don't tweak them every quarter.
points: Many campaigns can influence one opportunity
Auto-association via contact roles and campaign membership
Attribution models split revenue credit
Account Engagement adds first/last/even touch models

q: What is the difference between Account Teams and Opportunity Teams?
alt: Explain account teams vs opportunity teams
What is team selling in Salesforce?
how do you give extra users access to one account
What is a default opportunity team?
a: Both let you add users to a record with a role and an access level, but at different levels. An Account Team is the group that works an account over time, and you can give them read or edit access to the account and its related opportunities, cases and contacts. An Opportunity Team is specific to one deal. For example, for a big hospital customer, the account manager, a support rep and a technical lead sit on the account team year after year. When a large laptop refresh deal comes up, the rep adds a sales engineer and an executive sponsor to that one opportunity's team. Opportunity teams are also required if you want opportunity splits. Users can set a default opportunity team that gets added automatically to their new opportunities. Both kinds of team grant sharing on top of the org-wide defaults. So when I review a request to add teams, I look at it as a sharing change too, not just a UI feature.
points: Account team: long-term coverage of an account
Opportunity team: per deal, enables splits
Each member has a role and access level
Default teams can auto-add members

q: Two reps worked on the same deal and both need credit in the forecast. How would you handle it?
alt: How do opportunity splits work?
Give revenue credit to multiple users on one opportunity
revenue split vs overlay split
sales engineer needs credit for deals they support
a: I'd go with Opportunity Splits here, which need team selling enabled. Splits divide credit for an opportunity among opportunity team members by percentage. Revenue splits must total exactly 100 percent, so they're for when two reps truly share the deal. Overlay splits can add up to any percentage, and they're for supporting roles, like a sales engineer who gets credit without reducing the main rep's number. For example, on a 100,000 deal, Anil and Meera each get a 50 percent revenue split, so 50,000 each. The sales engineer gets a 20 percent overlay split, and Anil and Meera still keep their full 50,000. You can also create custom split types on other currency fields. Then I set up a forecast type based on opportunity splits, so each rep's share shows up in their forecast instead of the full amount going to the owner. Before building, I'd confirm the split rules with sales ops and finance, since splits often feed commissions and nobody wants surprises on payday.
points: Requires team selling and opportunity splits enabled
Revenue splits must total 100 percent
Overlay splits can exceed 100 percent
Use a split-based forecast type

q: What are Contact Roles on an opportunity?
alt: Explain opportunity contact roles
How do you track who is the decision maker on a deal?
what is primary contact role
Why do contact roles matter for campaign influence?
a: Opportunity Contact Roles link contacts to an opportunity and describe the part each person plays, like Decision Maker, Economic Buyer, Evaluator or Influencer. One contact can be marked as primary. It's a junction object, OpportunityContactRole, so a contact can be on many opportunities and an opportunity can have many contacts, and they don't have to belong to the same account. For example, on a laptop deal with a school, the principal is the Decision Maker, the bursar is the Economic Buyer, and an outside IT consultant from a different account is an Evaluator. It matters beyond tracking, because Customizable Campaign Influence uses contact roles to connect campaigns to opportunities. Many companies also add a validation or flow requiring at least one contact role before a deal moves to a later stage.
points: Junction object OpportunityContactRole
Role values describe buying influence
One primary contact role per opportunity
Used by campaign influence

q: What is the difference between a Task and an Event, and what are WhoId and WhatId?
alt: Explain activities in Salesforce
task vs event
what is who id and what id on activities
How are activities related to records?
a: Tasks and Events are both activities. A Task is a to-do with a due date and status, like a call to make or an email to send, and logged calls are tasks too. An Event is a calendar item with a start and end time, like a meeting. Both use two polymorphic lookups. WhoId points to a person, which is a Lead or Contact, and WhatId points to a thing, like an Account, Opportunity, Case or a custom object that allows activities. For example, a demo meeting with Sameer about a laptop deal has Sameer's contact as the WhoId and the opportunity as the WhatId. The gotcha: if WhoId is a lead, WhatId must be empty. And with Shared Activities enabled, one activity can be related to multiple contacts through TaskRelation and EventRelation.
points: Task = to-do with due date, Event = time-based meeting
WhoId = Lead or Contact, WhatId = other record
Lead on WhoId means WhatId must be blank
Shared Activities allows multiple contacts

q: What is Sales Engagement and what are cadences?
alt: Explain Salesforce Sales Engagement
What was High Velocity Sales?
how do sales cadences work
What is the work queue for inside sales reps?
a: Sales Engagement, formerly High Velocity Sales, is the Sales Cloud feature for inside sales and SDR teams to run structured outreach. The core is a cadence, which is a sequence of steps like a call, an email, a LinkedIn touch or wait a few days, with branching based on outcomes, like whether a call connected or an email got a reply. For example, step one is a call. If it connects, the lead goes to a follow-up email step. If not, the cadence waits two days and sends an intro email instead. Leads, contacts or person accounts are added as cadence targets, and reps work from a work queue that tells them exactly who to contact next and with which email template or call script. Managers can then report on which cadences and steps perform best.
points: Formerly High Velocity Sales
Cadence = ordered, branching outreach steps
Reps work from a prioritized work queue
Targets can be leads, contacts or person accounts

q: What AI features does Salesforce offer for sales teams today?
alt: Explain Einstein and Agentforce features in Sales Cloud
What is Agentforce SDR?
einstein lead scoring and opportunity scoring
How can AI help sales reps in Salesforce?
a: There are two layers. The predictive layer has Einstein Lead Scoring and Opportunity Scoring, which score records based on historical conversion and win patterns, plus Einstein Activity Capture, which syncs emails and calendar events from Gmail or Outlook. On top of that is the agent layer, where Einstein Copilot has become Agentforce, with agents built for sales. Agentforce SDR can work inbound leads on its own, answering questions, nurturing and booking meetings for reps. Agentforce Sales Coach lets a rep role-play a pitch or negotiation against the deal's context and get feedback. q: How would you design a lead routing process for a global sales team?
alt: Design lead assignment for multiple regions and product lines
How would you route inbound leads to the right rep fairly?
round robin lead assignment design
Leads should go to the right territory and be followed up quickly, how?
a: I start by agreeing the routing keys with sales ops, usually region, segment by company size, and product interest, plus any named-account rules. Then I clean and enrich the data on entry: normalize the country and state picklists, and run duplicate rules so existing customers go to their account owner. Next, the lead assignment rule sends leads to regional queues based on those keys. Inside each queue, a record-triggered flow or Omni-Channel does round robin or capacity-based distribution to available reps. Then I add an SLA, for example a scheduled path that alerts the manager or reassigns if a lead is untouched after a set time. Say a mid-size company in Germany asks about laptops. It lands in the Europe mid-market queue, goes round robin to the next available rep, and if nobody touches it within the SLA, the manager gets alerted. Finally I build a dashboard for speed-to-lead and conversion by source and rep.

q: How do you prevent users from closing an opportunity as Won if it has no products?

opportunity should not be closed won without product

a: The simplest answer is a validation rule on Opportunity using HasOpportunityLineItem, a checkbox Salesforce sets automatically when the opportunity has products. The rule fires when the stage is Closed Won and HasOpportunityLineItem is false, and shows a clear error telling the rep to add products first. So if a rep tries to close a laptop deal as Won with no products on it, the save is blocked with a message like: add at least one product before closing this deal. If the business needs something more specific, say at least one product from the Laptops family, I'd add a roll-up summary field counting those line items and check that count in the rule instead. I'd also make sure integrations or data loads that close deals are either compliant or have a controlled bypass.

q: Your company sells in USD, EUR and INR. How would you set up Sales Cloud for multi-currency deals?

What is advanced currency management?
dated exchange rates for opportunities
Deals in different currencies but reports in USD, how?
a: I'd enable multi-currency, which adds a CurrencyIsoCode field to records, set the corporate currency, say USD, and add EUR and INR as active currencies with conversion rates. Each user has a personal currency and each opportunity has its own currency, and reports convert amounts to the user's or corporate currency. Price book entries must exist per currency, because an opportunity can only use entries in its own currency. So if a laptop only has a USD entry, a rep on an INR deal won't see it. If finance needs historical accuracy, I'd enable Advanced Currency Management for dated exchange rates. Those apply to opportunities, opportunity products, schedules and related reports, but not to most other objects, or to roll-up summary fields in the same way. The key point is that multi-currency can't be disabled once enabled, so I test it in a sandbox first.

how do you give two teams different opportunity layouts and stages

Say a laptop seller has a hardware team that ships devices and a services team that sells repair contracts. Hardware might need a Demo stage, services might need a Site Survey stage, and each rep only sees their own. Each record type gets its own page layout or Lightning record page and its own Path with key fields and guidance. If needed I also add different lead processes and validation rules scoped by record type, and reports can be filtered by record type to compare the two units.

q: Web-to-Lead is creating lots of duplicate leads. How would you fix it?
alt: How do you stop duplicate leads in Salesforce?
Duplicate rules and matching rules for leads
same person submitting form multiple times creating duplicates
existing contacts coming in again as new leads
a: I'd set up matching rules and duplicate rules on Lead, matching on email, or on name plus company, and include a rule that checks existing Contacts too. A customer filling the form again shouldn't become a brand-new lead. Say someone who already bought ten laptops fills the enquiry form again for more. Web-to-Lead doesn't show the visitor any alert, so I set the duplicate rule action to allow and report. Then a flow handles it: it links the new lead to the existing record, updates it, or routes it to the current owner, so the person's existing rep gets the enquiry. For high-volume forms I'd move to an API or Flow-based intake that does an upsert or match before creating anything. And a periodic merge job or tool cleans up the duplicates that already exist.

q: When an opportunity is Closed Won, the business wants a renewal opportunity created automatically. How would you build it?
alt: Auto create renewal opportunity on closed won
Create a follow-up opportunity one year later
flow to clone opportunity when won
Automate renewals in Sales Cloud
a: I'd build an after-save record-triggered flow on Opportunity, with the entry condition that the stage changed to Closed Won and the type is new business or subscription. The flow creates a new opportunity on the same account with type Renewal, the same owner, a stage like Prospecting, and a close date one year after the original close date or the contract end date. Say a company buys a one-year laptop support plan that closes on 15 March. The flow creates a Renewal opportunity closing 15 March next year. If products need to carry over, the flow gets the original OpportunityLineItems and creates copies on the new opportunity, using the same price book. The gotcha is duplicates: if the deal is reopened and closed again, you'd get a second renewal, so I store a lookup to the original opportunity and check it. And I test it with bulk data loads.

Lookup to source opportunity prevents duplicates

q: A sales manager says an opportunity is missing from the forecast. How would you troubleshoot it?
alt: Opportunity not showing in collaborative forecast
Why is my deal not in the forecast rollup?
forecast amount does not match pipeline report
rep's opportunity missing from manager forecast
a: I'd check a few things in order. First, the close date has to fall in the forecast period being viewed, and the forecast category can't be Omitted. Second, the opportunity owner must be enabled for forecasting and sit under that manager in the forecast hierarchy, which is separate from just being in the role hierarchy. Third, the forecast type: if it's based on splits or product families, the deal only shows up if splits or products exist. For example, a manager is looking at a product-family forecast and a rep's 40,000 laptop deal is missing. Often the deal simply has no products added yet, so there's nothing to roll up. In multi-currency orgs, the amount shows converted, which can look like a mismatch. I also confirm the manager has access, and if territories are used, that the opportunity has a territory in the active model.

prevent lead convert unless budget and timeline are filled

The gotcha is that lead validation rules only run during conversion if Require Validation for Converted Leads is enabled in Lead Settings, so I make sure that's on. For a better experience, I also show those fields on the Path for the Qualified stage, so the rep knows what's needed before clicking Convert.

get opportunities and opportunity products in one query

I filter on IsClosed false to get open deals, and I use a bind variable for the account or owner instead of hard-coding Ids. q: A sales rep left the company. How do you reassign their accounts, opportunities and leads?
alt: Transfer records when a user leaves
Mass transfer accounts to another rep
what to do with records of a deactivated sales user
How do you move all open deals to a new owner?
a: First I'd freeze the user so they can't log in while we plan. Deactivating can be blocked if they're used in places like default lead owner or an approval process. Then I use Mass Transfer Records, or the Transfer Account option, to move accounts to the new owner, choosing whether to also move open opportunities, cases and the rep's open activities. Leads can go to the new rep or back to a queue. For large volumes I use Data Loader: export, change the owner, update. Say Rohit leaves with 300 accounts and 2,000 leads. I'd transfer his accounts with their open deals to Neha, send the leads back to the regional queue, and then check account and opportunity teams, territories, assignment rules, queues, and any flows or reports that still reference Rohit. Only after that cleanup do I deactivate him.

q: What is a queue, and why would you assign leads to a queue instead of a user?

how do queues work for leads

Can a queue own a record?
a: A queue is a holding place that can own records, like leads or cases, and it has a set of members who can pick records from it. Assigning leads to a queue makes sense when you don't want to decide the exact rep upfront. For example, all inbound leads for the APAC region go to an APAC queue, and whichever rep is free accepts the lead and becomes the owner. So if three reps cover APAC and one is on leave, nothing sits stuck in that person's name. Members see the queue as a list view, and you can set a queue email to notify them. Queues also work with Omni-Channel, which can push records from a queue to available reps automatically, instead of reps picking them manually.

q: The business has different prices for distributors, direct customers and different regions. How would you design the price books?
alt: Price book strategy for regional and partner pricing
How many price books should we create?
design pricing in sales cloud for channels
Different price lists for different customer types
a: I'd keep one product catalog and model the price differences with custom price books, one per channel and region combination that really has a different list price, rather than duplicating products. Each price book has entries for the products it sells, in each currency it supports. For example, a laptop seller might have Distributor India, Direct India and Direct Europe, and the same laptop product sits in all three at different prices. Then I control which price book a rep can use with price book sharing, and I default it automatically, like a flow that sets Pricebook2Id on the opportunity based on the account's channel and region field. Discounts on top of list price go through an approval process. If the pricing becomes rule-heavy, with tiers, bundles or contract pricing, I'd move to Revenue Cloud instead of exploding the number of price books.

q: Any discount above 20 percent on an opportunity must be approved by the sales manager. How would you implement this?
alt: Discount approval process on opportunity
How to require manager approval for big discounts
approval process when discount is more than 20 percent
Lock the opportunity until the discount is approved
a: I'd add a discount field, or calculate the overall discount from line items with a roll-up, and create an approval process on Opportunity with entry criteria that the discount is greater than 20 percent. The approver is the submitter's manager, using the manager field on the user. While it's pending, the record is locked. On approval I set an approved flag and status, and on rejection I reset it. Say a rep offers a school 25 percent off 40 laptops. They submit it, it goes to their manager, and the deal is locked until she decides. To make sure reps can't skip it, I add a validation rule that blocks moving to Closed Won or syncing a quote when the discount is above 20 percent and not approved. I'd also consider the newer Flow Approvals if the org has standardized on Flow orchestration.

q: What is the difference between Sales Cloud and Service Cloud?

Which features come with Service Cloud but not Sales Cloud?
explain sales cloud and service cloud in simple words

a: Sales Cloud is about winning business: leads, opportunities, products, price books, quotes, forecasts, territories and campaigns. Service Cloud is about supporting customers after the sale: cases, entitlements and milestones, Knowledge, Omni-Channel routing, the service console, chat and messaging channels, voice and service agents. Both share the core objects like accounts and contacts. Basic cases exist in Sales Cloud editions too, but advanced service features like entitlement management, Omni-Channel and Knowledge need Service Cloud licensing. Think of a laptop seller: the sales team uses Sales Cloud to close a 200-laptop deal, and when one of those laptops won't boot, the support desk handles that case in Service Cloud. Many companies use both, so a sales rep can see open cases on an account before a renewal call.

q: What is Path, and how does it help sales reps?
alt: Explain Sales Path in Lightning
How do you show guidance for each opportunity stage?
what is path in salesforce lightning
key fields and guidance for success
a: Path is the chevron bar at the top of a Lightning record page that shows each stage or status of a record, like opportunity stage or lead status. For each step you can configure key fields, which the rep can fill right from the path, and guidance for success, which is short text, links or tips on what to do at that stage. For example, on the Proposal stage of a laptop deal, the key fields could be Budget and Decision Date, with guidance like: confirm delivery dates before sending the quote. You can create a path per record type, so different sales processes get different guidance, and you can turn on confetti when a deal reaches Closed Won. It's a simple way to make the sales process visible and push data quality without forcing everything through validation rules.

Works for any picklist, including custom objects

q: Sales leadership wants better pipeline visibility and fewer surprises at quarter end. What would you put in place?
alt: How do you improve forecast accuracy in Sales Cloud?
Design pipeline management for sales leaders
pipeline inspection and deal health
Managers can't see which deals are slipping, what would you build?
a: I'd start with data discipline: clear stage definitions with exit criteria on the Path, required fields at key stages, and a stage-to-forecast-category mapping everyone agrees on. Then Collaborative Forecasts with the right forecast type and quotas loaded, so managers see Commit and Best Case against target and can adjust. Pipeline Inspection shows changes, like deals that moved close dates, changed amounts or changed stages this week, and that's where slipping deals show up. For example, if a big laptop deal has pushed its close date three weeks in a row, the manager sees it on Monday instead of on the last day of the quarter. Opportunity scoring can flag risky deals. Finally I add historical trend reporting for pipeline coverage and win rate, plus a weekly review cadence. The tooling only works if stage definitions are enforced, so that part comes first.

Opportunity scoring and trend reporting

q: What is a Case in Service Cloud and what is a support process?
alt: Explain the case lifecycle
What are case status and case origin?
what is support process in salesforce
How do cases get created and closed?
a: A Case is a customer issue, question or request, and it's the core record in Service Cloud. Agents can create cases, or they come in automatically through channels like email, web forms, chat, messaging or phone. Each case has fields like Status, Priority, Origin, Type and Reason, and links to a Contact and Account. A support process is the set of Case Status values a team uses, like a sales process for opportunities, and you assign it through case record types. At least one status is marked as closed. Say a customer emails a laptop seller's support desk because their screen flickers. That becomes a case with Origin Email, it moves through statuses like New, Working and Waiting on Customer, and when it's fixed the agent closes it. Then you can report on resolution time and first contact resolution.

q: What are case assignment rules?
alt: How do you auto assign cases to queues?
Explain case assignment rules
how many active case assignment rules
How does a new case get the right owner?
a: Case assignment rules set the case owner automatically to a user or a queue, based on criteria like product, priority, origin or customer region. Only one case assignment rule can be active, and its entries are evaluated in order until the first match. For example, at a laptop seller's support desk, entry one sends high-priority cases from business customers to the Premium queue, and entry two sends everything about batteries to the Hardware queue. The rules fire for email-to-case, web-to-case and other channels, and for manual creation when the assignment checkbox is used. If no entry matches, the case goes to the default case owner in Support Settings. In most modern setups the rule sends the case to a queue, and then Omni-Channel pushes it to an available agent.

q: What are escalation rules and how do they work?

How do you escalate a case that is not resolved in time?
escalation rule age over hours
What happens when a case is escalated?
a: Escalation rules automatically escalate cases that aren't handled within a set time. Only one escalation rule can be active, with ordered entries that define which cases qualify, like high-priority cases from premium customers. Each entry has escalation actions based on age, like reassign to a senior queue, notify a manager, or both. Say a business customer logs a high-priority case at 4 pm about laptops that won't boot. If the rule says escalate after four hours and respects business hours, and support closes at 6 pm, it won't escalate overnight; the clock picks up the next morning. Age can be measured from case creation or last modification. When it fires, the case's IsEscalated flag is set. For proper contractual SLAs I prefer entitlements and milestones, and I use escalation rules for simpler internal escalation.

Actions by age: reassign and/or notify
Can respect business hours
Sets IsEscalated on the case

q: What are auto-response rules?

Explain auto response rules
auto response rule vs workflow email
Send a thank you email for web to case
a: Auto-response rules send an automatic email to the customer when a case or lead is created through web-to-case, email-to-case or web-to-lead, usually to confirm the request was received and share the case number. Only one auto-response rule can be active per object, and like assignment rules, its entries are evaluated in order. The first matching entry decides which email template is sent and from which address. So at a laptop seller's support desk, premium customers could get a reply from the priority support address saying someone will call within the hour, while everyone else gets the standard acknowledgement. They don't fire for cases created manually by agents, so if an agent logs a phone call as a case, no auto-response goes out. For anything more complex, like conditional follow-ups later, I'd use a flow.

q: What is the difference between Email-to-Case and On-Demand Email-to-Case?

how does email to case work

a: Both turn customer emails into cases. On-Demand Email-to-Case is the standard approach today. You set up routing addresses in Salesforce, and the support mailbox forwards emails to a Salesforce-generated service address, so nothing is installed and Salesforce's own email services process the mail. That's useful when security rules don't allow forwarding mail outside, or when attachments are very large. For example, a laptop seller forwards support@ to the Salesforce address, and for that routing address sets origin Email, priority Medium and the Tier 1 queue as defaults. Then users add members to a case manually, or you set up predefined case teams that get added automatically, for example through assignment rules or a flow. q: Explain Entitlements, Entitlement Processes and Milestones.

a: An Entitlement defines what support a customer gets, like 24/7 phone support or a four-hour response, and it's usually linked to an account, asset or service contract. At three hours a warning emails the team lead, and if four hours pass, the violation action fires. Cases show a milestone tracker, and each one is stored as a CaseMilestone record you can report on.

q: What is Omni-Channel and what are its main components?

a: Omni-Channel is Salesforce's routing engine. It pushes work items, like cases, chats, messaging sessions, leads or custom objects, to the right available agent, instead of agents picking from queues. The main pieces are service channels, which define which object is routed; routing configurations, which set priority, the routing model like least active or most available, and how much capacity each item uses; queues or skills that hold the work; presence statuses like Available for Cases; and presence configurations, which set agent capacity and behavior like auto-accept. For example, at a laptop seller's support desk, a new case lands in the Hardware queue and Omni-Channel offers it to the least busy hardware agent who's online. Agents use the Omni-Channel widget in the console to go online and accept work, and supervisors watch it all in the Omni Supervisor app.

q: What is the difference between queue-based routing and skills-based routing in Omni-Channel?

When would you use skills-based routing?

a: In queue-based routing, work goes into a queue linked to a routing configuration, and Omni-Channel pushes it to any available member of that queue. It's simple and works well when teams are clearly split. q: A case comes in by email from a contact who is not in Salesforce. What happens, and how would you handle it?
alt: Email to case from unknown sender
How does email-to-case link contact and account?

a: Email-to-Case tries to match the sender's email address to an existing contact. If it finds exactly one, it sets ContactId, and the account comes from that contact. If there's no match, or more than one, the case is created without a contact, and the email is stored in the Web Email field. Say someone new at a customer company emails support about a laptop. There's no contact for her, so the case just has her address in Web Email. To handle it, I'd add a flow or Apex on case creation: if ContactId is blank, look for a contact by email, and if none exists, create a contact under a placeholder or matched-by-domain account, or flag the case for the agent to link manually. Matching by email domain to an account can help in B2B, but I'd confirm that rule with the business first.
